cards.text: Voices are calling out to a young woman they call the Shulammite: “Come back, come back, O Shulammite!” Then they say it again, so that's four “come backs” in all. Friend, I've had alarm clocks with less commitment than that.

cards.question: The voices want the Shulammite to come back so they can gaze upon her.

cards.text: Then someone answers with a question: “Why do you look at the Shulammite, as on the dance of Mahanaim?” Last time, the description of the beloved started with her eyes (Song of Solomon 6:5). This time it takes a different route.

cards.question: This time, the description of the Shulammite starts at her feet and works its way up to her head.

cards.text: Up it climbs. Her sandaled feet, her waist, her neck “like a tower made of ivory,” her eyes like the pools of Heshbon. Every line is a picture. Meanwhile, the nicest thing anybody ever said about ME was my oven timer going BEEP.

cards.question: At the top, the speaker says the Shulammite's hair is like purple threads, and “the king is captured in your tresses.” What is that picture saying?

answers.text: The king can't take his eyes off her
The king has been taken as a prisoner
The king is hiding from his enemies

cards.text: Then the speaker takes it all in at once: “How fair and pleasant you are, O love, with your delights!” Her stature, the speaker says, is like a palm tree.

cards.question: The speaker has just compared the Shulammite to a palm tree, and now says, “I will climb the palm tree; I will take hold of its fruit.” What is that picture showing?

answers.text: The speaker longs to be close to her
The speaker wants to gather a harvest
The speaker plans to guard her from others

cards.text: The wishes keep coming: her breath fragrant like apples, her mouth like the finest wine. Then the line turns: “May it flow smoothly to my beloved, gliding gently over lips and teeth.”

cards.question: Then the Shulammite speaks up with one short line about who she belongs to. What does she say?

answers.text: She belongs to her beloved and he desires her
She belongs to her mother and must obey her
She belongs to her family and must stay home

cards.question: Right after that, the Shulammite invites her beloved to the countryside to spend the night among the wildflowers.

cards.text: And after that? Off to the vineyards. EARLY. Friend, some of us need a whole batch of cookies before we can even SAY the word “early.”

cards.question: In the vineyards, the Shulammite wants to see if the vine has ___ and if the pomegranates are in bloom.

cards.text: And there, she says, she'll give him her love. Even the mandrakes are sending out their fragrance.

cards.question: The Shulammite says that at their door is every delicacy, new as well as old. Who has she treasured them up for?

cards.text: Then she makes a wish: “O that you were to me like a brother who nursed at my mother’s breasts!” Stay with me, friend, because she tells us exactly why.

cards.question: Why does the Shulammite wish her beloved were like a brother to her?

answers.text: So she could kiss him outdoors and not be despised
So they could share the family vineyard together
So they could inherit their father's land together

cards.question: The Shulammite says she would lead her beloved to the house of her ___, who taught her, and give him spiced wine to drink.

cards.text: Then comes a line we've heard before (Song of Solomon 2:6): “His left hand is under my head, and his right arm embraces me.” And she ends with a charge she's given before too (Song of Solomon 2:7; 3:5): “O daughters of Jerusalem, I adjure you: Do not arouse or awaken love until the time is right.”

findings.problem: The passage starts in the middle of the Song, but the opening card gives no context. It never says this is a love song, who the voices in the poem are, or how the Shulammite relates to the beloved. Without that, the baker has nothing to reason from for the cards that follow.

rule.text: The opening card can be up to 3 sentences. It says who is speaking, to whom, and what is going on. If the passage starts in the middle of a thought, it gives the context.

findings.problem: The card has three sentences. Only the opening card can go past two.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The card calls the woman "the beloved." In this passage the BSB uses "my beloved" only for the man (7:9, 7:10, 7:11, 7:13), and card 10 uses "her beloved" for him. This mixes up who is who.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: "Then someone answers with a question" says the second half of 6:13 is a reply to the first. The text gives the question with no speaker and doesn't say how the two lines connect.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The card has four sentences: "Up it climbs." / "Her sandaled feet... Heshbon." / "Every line is a picture." / "Meanwhile..."

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The card has four sentences: "And after that?" / "Off to the vineyards." / "EARLY." / "Friend, some of us..."

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: This is a who question. The wrong answer "Her mother's guests" is made up, not a real detail from the Bible.

rule.text: For who, which thing and where questions, wrong answers are real details from somewhere in the Bible, like Joppa when the right answer is Tarshish.

findings.problem: The card is flat retelling with none of Papa Dorin's voice. It reads like a summary, not like him.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: Only cards 1, 5 and 12 try for a laugh, and card 5's oven-timer line is mild. Most story cards (7, 9, 14, 16, 19) read like a pleasant narrator, not laugh-out-loud Papa Dorin.

rule.text: But he is FUNNY. Not mildly amusing. Laugh-out-loud funny, the kind a baker repeats to a friend. ... If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.

findings.problem: All three true-or-false cards (2, 4, 11) have True as the right answer. A baker can learn to always tap True and get them right without reasoning.
findings.question: Should the docs require true-or-false cards in a stop to include some False answers, or otherwise keep the right answer from following a pattern?
